stem: What distinguishes supervised from unsupervised learning?
correct: Supervised learning fits a map from inputs to observed labels; unsupervised learning has inputs only.
Only the supervised setting provides target values $y$ to learn from.

distractors.text: Supervised learning always predicts a continuous quantity, while unsupervised learning predicts classes.
distractors.misconception: confuses the learning setting with regression versus classification

distractors.text: Unsupervised learning needs more labelled data than supervised learning because it must discover the labels.
Supervised learning uses a loss function, while unsupervised learning has no objective at all.
distractors.misconception: believes unsupervised methods have no objective

distractors.text: The two differ only in the algorithm used, not in the data that is available.
distractors.misconception: ignores the presence or absence of labels

distractors.text: Supervised learning requires a linear model, and unsupervised learning requires a nonlinear one.
distractors.misconception: ties the setting to model class

explanation: Regression and classification are both supervised. Clustering and dimension reduction are unsupervised, as they have no labels $y$ to match.

stem: Why is the training error a biased estimate of the test error?
correct: The model was fitted to this very data, so it scores better here than on new data.
The same observations both fit the model and score it, so the error is optimistic.

distractors.text: The training set is always smaller than the test set, so its error is smaller.
The test error is computed with a different loss function from the training error.
distractors.misconception: invents a mismatch in the loss

distractors.text: The training error is pessimistic, because fitted models underfit the data they see.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the bias

distractors.text: Training error is biased only for nonlinear models, and unbiased for linear ones.
The bias disappears as the model gets more complex.
distractors.misconception: reverses the effect of complexity on optimism

explanation: Fitting uses the training labels, so for flexible models the training error is far below the error on fresh data. Held-out data are needed for an honest estimate.

stem: How does the expected squared test error of a predictor decompose?
correct: Squared bias plus variance of the fit plus the irreducible noise variance.
$E(y-\hat f(x))^2=\text{bias}^2+\text{variance}+\sigma^2$, where $\sigma^2$ cannot be removed.

distractors.text: Bias plus variance, where the bias enters unsquared and there is no noise term.
distractors.misconception: drops the square and the noise term

distractors.text: Bias times variance plus the noise variance.
Variance only, since the bias vanishes for large samples.
distractors.misconception: believes the bias disappears with data

distractors.text: Squared bias minus variance plus noise, since variance reduces the error.
Squared bias plus variance, with the noise term removed by a better model.

explanation: More flexible models have lower bias and higher variance; the noise $\sigma^2$ is a floor that no model can go below.

stem: Which pattern signals overfitting?
correct: Training error keeps falling while validation error starts to rise.
A widening gap between low training error and higher held-out error.

distractors.text: Training and validation errors are both high and close to each other.
Validation error is lower than training error and both fall together.
Training error rises while validation error falls.
Both errors are exactly zero.
distractors.misconception: treats perfect fit as a test-set result

distractors.text: The validation error is constant whatever the complexity.
distractors.misconception: describes a model that ignores the inputs

explanation: Overfitting means fitting noise: more capacity keeps lowering training error, but held-out error eventually rises.

stem: What is the irreducible error in a prediction problem?
correct: The outcome's spread around its best prediction, which no model can remove.
Noise in $y$ given $x$, a floor on error.

distractors.text: The error caused by using too simple a model, which more data would remove.
distractors.misconception: describes bias, which can be reduced

distractors.text: The error caused by a small training set, which disappears with more data.
The error of the best model in the class on the training set.
distractors.misconception: confuses irreducible error with training error

distractors.text: The error that arises from rounding in the computer.
distractors.misconception: confuses statistical noise with numerical error

distractors.text: The error that regularisation always removes.

explanation: Even the true regression function leaves $\operatorname{Var}(y\mid x)$ unexplained. In finance, this noise is very large relative to the signal.

stem: How are the least squares coefficients of a linear model characterised?
correct: They solve the normal equations $X^\top X\beta=X^\top y$, zeroing the gradient.
At the optimum the residual vector is orthogonal to every column of $X$.

distractors.text: They minimise the sum of absolute residuals, which is robust to outliers.
They maximise the correlation between $X$ and $y$ for each column separately.
distractors.misconception: replaces joint fitting by marginal correlations

distractors.text: They always equal the average of $y$ for every feature.
distractors.misconception: confuses the fit with the sample mean

distractors.text: They are found by an iterative procedure because no closed form exists.
distractors.misconception: ignores the closed form of the normal equations

distractors.text: They make the residuals have unit variance.

explanation: The squared loss is a quadratic in $\beta$, so its minimiser has a closed form when $X^\top X$ is invertible; the residual is orthogonal to the column space of $X$.

stem: What is the logistic loss for a binary classifier with predicted probability $p_i$ and label $y_i\in\{0,1\}$?
correct: The negative log-likelihood of the labels.
Bernoulli cross-entropy.

distractors.text: The squared difference $\sum(y_i-p_i)^2$ between labels and probabilities.
The number of misclassified observations at the 0.5 threshold.
$\sum\max(0,1-y_if_i)$ with labels in $\{-1,1\}$.
The sum of the absolute differences between labels and probabilities.
The log of the predicted probability of the wrong class.

explanation: Minimising the logistic loss is maximum likelihood for the Bernoulli model. It is convex in the weights and penalises confident wrong predictions heavily.

stem: In gradient descent $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla L(\theta)$, what is the effect of the learning rate $\eta$?
correct: A step too large can overshoot and diverge; one too small crawls.
It scales each step, balancing stability against speed of progress.

distractors.text: It has no effect on convergence, only on the final accuracy.
distractors.misconception: ignores the effect of step size on stability

distractors.text: A larger $\eta$ always converges faster, as steps are bigger.
The learning rate must be negative to move downhill.
distractors.misconception: confuses the sign of the step with the sign of the rate

distractors.text: It must equal the number of observations.
distractors.misconception: invents a relation to the sample size

distractors.text: Smaller steps make the loss rise, because the gradient is evaluated less often.

explanation: For a quadratic loss with largest curvature $L$, gradient descent converges if $\eta<2/L$ and diverges beyond it.

stem: For logistic regression with weights $w$ and predicted probabilities $p_i$, what form does the gradient of the average loss take?
correct: $\frac1nX^\top(p-y)$, the features weighted by the prediction errors.
A sum of feature vectors times the residuals $p_i-y_i$.

distractors.text: $\frac1nX^\top(y-p)^2$, the squared errors.
$\frac1n(p-y)$ with no dependence on the features.
$\frac1nX^\top p(1-p)$, the variance of each prediction.
distractors.misconception: confuses the gradient with the weights of the Hessian

distractors.text: $\frac1n\sum\log p_i$, the average log probability.
distractors.misconception: gives the loss, not its gradient

distractors.text: Zero at every parameter value, because the model is probabilistic.

explanation: The gradient is $X^\top(p-y)/n$. The Hessian $X^\top\operatorname{diag}\{p_i(1-p_i)\}X/n$ is positive semidefinite, so the loss is convex.

stem: What is true of gradient descent on the logistic loss for a linearly separable data set?
correct: The loss only tends to zero as the weights grow without bound.
No finite minimiser exists.

distractors.text: It converges to a unique finite minimiser, as the loss is convex.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that convexity does not guarantee a minimiser

distractors.text: The weights oscillate, since separable data make the gradient change sign.
It cannot decrease the loss, because the classifier is already perfect.
The loss becomes negative after enough steps.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the cross-entropy is nonnegative

distractors.text: It converges only if the learning rate is set to one.

explanation: Regularisation (or early stopping) keeps the weights finite: with an $L_2$ penalty the minimiser exists and is unique.

stem: How do ridge and lasso penalties differ in their effect on a linear model?
correct: Ridge shrinks coefficients smoothly; lasso can set some exactly to zero.
The $L_1$ penalty gives sparse solutions and the $L_2$ penalty does not.

distractors.text: Lasso shrinks all coefficients by the same factor, and ridge sets small ones to zero.
Both penalties give exactly the same solutions.
distractors.misconception: ignores the difference between the norms

distractors.text: Ridge performs variable selection, while lasso is unaffected by collinearity.
The $L_2$ penalty is not convex, and the $L_1$ penalty is.
Lasso increases the variance of coefficient estimates compared with least squares.

explanation: Ridge keeps all predictors with smaller coefficients; the lasso is useful for selection but can be unstable among correlated predictors.

stem: How does a larger regularisation parameter $\lambda$ change a penalised regression fit?
correct: It raises bias and lowers variance.
Coefficients shrink harder, giving a simpler model with higher training error.

distractors.text: It lowers bias and raises variance.
It lowers both bias and variance, so the largest $\lambda$ is best.
It does not change the training error.
distractors.misconception: ignores that shrinkage worsens the training fit

distractors.text: It increases the flexibility of the model, since coefficients are free to move.
It makes the fitted model identical to the least squares fit.

explanation: $\lambda=0$ gives least squares; as $\lambda\to\infty$ the coefficients tend to zero (the intercept-only model).

stem: How does $K$-fold cross-validation estimate the prediction error?
correct: Split into $K$ parts, train on $K-1$, score the held-out part, average the scores.
Each observation is validated exactly once, and the held-out errors are averaged.

distractors.text: It trains on all the data and scores on the same data $K$ times.
It scores the model on $K$ different random subsets of the training data, including the points it was trained on.
distractors.misconception: lets training points leak into the validation set

distractors.text: It trains on one part and scores on the remaining $K-1$ parts.
distractors.misconception: reverses the roles of training and validation sets

distractors.text: It fits $K$ models with different penalties and picks the one with the lowest training error.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with picking by training error

distractors.text: It requires an extra test set to be defined.
distractors.misconception: believes the method needs a separate test set to run

explanation: Averaging over folds reduces the variance of the estimate. A final test set is still needed to assess a model whose $\lambda$ was tuned on the folds.

stem: Why must a final test set stay untouched while hyperparameters are tuned?
correct: Picking the best of many settings on test data makes the error optimistic.
Tuning on it leaks information.

distractors.text: The test set is needed to compute the training error.
distractors.misconception: confuses the roles of the data sets

distractors.text: A used test set loses its labels, so it cannot score again.
Test data are too small to tune on, but otherwise tuning on them is fine.
distractors.misconception: treats the problem as only one of size

distractors.text: Tuning on the test set raises the variance but does not bias the estimate.
Test data may only be used once per day.

explanation: Selection of the minimum over many candidates biases the winner's score downward. Keep a separate test set, or use nested cross-validation.

stem: Compared with 5-fold cross-validation, what is a property of leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV)?
correct: Lower bias, but $n$ fits are needed.
Training sets almost as large as the full data.

distractors.text: It has higher bias because the training sets are smaller.
It needs only a single model fit for any model.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the linear smoother shortcut

distractors.text: It is always unbiased for the future error.
It uses fewer observations for training than 5-fold CV.
It cannot be used for ridge regression.

explanation: For linear smoothers the LOOCV error has a closed form $\frac1n\sum\{(y_i-\hat y_i)/(1-h_{ii})\}^2$, so one fit suffices in that case.

stem: What does a $k$-nearest-neighbour classifier predict for a new point?
correct: The majority class among the $k$ training points closest to it.
A vote of its $k$ nearest neighbours in the feature space.

distractors.text: The class of the training point with the largest feature values.
The majority class of the whole training set.
The average of the labels of all training points weighted equally.
The class given by a fitted linear boundary.
The class of the $k$ farthest points.

explanation: A small $k$ gives a flexible boundary with low bias and high variance; $k=n$ predicts the global majority class.

stem: Why do distance-based methods such as $k$-NN degrade in high dimensions?
correct: Distances concentrate, so the nearest and farthest points are almost equally far.
Data become sparse, and the "near" neighbours are no longer local.

distractors.text: Distances become exactly zero, so all points are neighbours.
High-dimensional distances cannot be computed.
distractors.misconception: confuses a statistical issue with a computational limit

distractors.text: The nearest neighbours become more informative as dimension grows.
The training set grows with the dimension, so the method is slower but unaffected in accuracy.
Only the Euclidean distance degrades; other distances stay informative at any dimension.

explanation: To keep neighbours local the sample size must grow exponentially in the dimension, which is the curse of dimensionality.

stem: What condition makes a function $k(x,x')$ a valid kernel?
correct: Its Gram matrices are positive semidefinite.
It is an inner product of feature maps, so every Gram matrix is symmetric PSD.

distractors.text: It is symmetric and nonnegative, whatever its Gram matrices look like.
It decreases with the distance between $x$ and $x'$.
distractors.misconception: mistakes a property of some kernels for the condition

distractors.text: It has values in the interval $[0,1]$.
distractors.misconception: confuses a kernel with a similarity score

distractors.text: It is the difference of two feature maps.
distractors.misconception: replaces the inner product by a difference

distractors.text: It is positive definite only for points in the training set.
distractors.misconception: restricts the condition to the sample

explanation: Mercer's condition: positive semidefinite Gram matrices for every finite set of points, so $k(x,x')=\langle\varphi(x),\varphi(x')\rangle$ for some $\varphi$.

stem: Why should features be standardised before applying $k$-NN?
correct: Large-scale features would dominate the distance and swamp the others.
Distances depend on units, so rescaling puts features on a common footing.

distractors.text: Standardising makes the labels balanced across classes.
$k$-NN needs features with mean zero in order to be defined.
Standardising removes the curse of dimensionality.
It is only needed when the features are categorical.
It is unnecessary because the nearest neighbour does not change under scaling of a single feature.
distractors.misconception: forgets that scaling a feature changes the metric

explanation: Euclidean distance weighs a feature by its scale. A feature in dollars would swamp one in per cent unless both are rescaled.

stem: What does the Cover-Hart result say about the nearest-neighbour classifier?
correct: Asymptotically its error is at most twice the Bayes error.
Error is bounded by twice the optimum.

distractors.text: Asymptotically its error equals the Bayes error exactly.
Its error is at least twice the Bayes error.
Its error is bounded by the training error divided by two.
It is optimal for any sample size.
Its error rate is independent of the Bayes error rate.

explanation: For two classes, $R^*\le R_{1NN}\le2R^*(1-R^*)$. Letting $k\to\infty$ with $k/n\to0$ gives the Bayes error.

stem: What is the margin of a linear classifier $f(x)=w^\top x+b$ in a support vector machine with canonical scaling?
correct: The width $2/\|w\|$, which the SVM maximises.
The distance between the hyperplanes $w^\top x+b=\pm1$.

distractors.text: The number of correctly classified points.
The value of $b$, the intercept of the boundary.
distractors.misconception: confuses the margin with the offset

distractors.text: The width $\|w\|/2$, which the SVM maximises.
The distance of the farthest point from the boundary.
distractors.misconception: uses the farthest rather than the nearest point

distractors.text: The training error of the classifier.
distractors.misconception: confuses the margin with the error

explanation: Maximising $2/\|w\|$ is equivalent to minimising $\tfrac12\|w\|^2$ subject to $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1$.

stem: Which training points are support vectors of an SVM?
correct: Points on or inside the margin; only they fix the solution.
Those with nonzero dual coefficients.

distractors.text: All the points of the minority class.
distractors.misconception: confuses support vectors with class imbalance

distractors.text: The points farthest from the boundary.
Every point misclassified by an unconstrained linear fit.
Exactly the points at the centre of each class.
Only the points exactly on the margin, never those inside it.
distractors.misconception: ignores margin violations in the soft margin case

explanation: Points strictly outside the margin have dual coefficient zero. The classifier depends only on support vectors.

stem: In the soft-margin SVM with hinge loss $\max(0,1-y_if(x_i))$ and penalty $C$, what does a larger $C$ do?
correct: Margin violations cost more, so the margin narrows and the fit may overfit.
Fewer violations are tolerated.

distractors.text: It widens the margin and allows more violations.
It has no effect on the solution, only on the speed.
It switches the loss from hinge to squared error.
distractors.misconception: confuses a parameter with the choice of loss

distractors.text: It makes the SVM equal to the nearest neighbour classifier.
It restricts the weights to be sparse.
distractors.misconception: confuses the SVM with the lasso

explanation: The objective $\tfrac12\|w\|^2+C\sum\xi_i$ balances margin against violations; $C\to\infty$ gives the hard-margin SVM.

stem: What does the kernel trick allow in an SVM?
correct: Nonlinear boundaries from inner products, without computing the feature map.
Kernels replace inner products in the dual.

distractors.text: It lets the SVM handle unlabelled data.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a semi-supervised method

distractors.text: It reduces the number of training points.
It makes the problem non-convex so that it can fit more complicated boundaries.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the dual remains convex

distractors.text: It removes the need for the margin.
distractors.misconception: misstates the role of the kernel

distractors.text: It computes the feature map exactly in a lower dimension.
distractors.misconception: believes the feature space is smaller

explanation: With an RBF kernel the implicit feature space is infinite-dimensional, yet the dual only needs the $n\times n$ Gram matrix.

stem: For the RBF kernel $k(x,x')=\exp(-\gamma\|x-x'\|^2)$, what is the effect of a very large $\gamma$?
correct: Each point influences only a tiny neighbourhood, so the boundary overfits.
Nearly memorises the data.

distractors.text: The boundary becomes nearly linear.
All points become equally similar.
The classifier underfits, ignoring local structure.
The margin disappears, so the classifier cannot be trained.
It acts like a penalty on the weights.
distractors.misconception: confuses the kernel width with regularisation

explanation: Large $\gamma$ means narrow bumps, high variance and low bias; small $\gamma$ gives a smooth near-linear boundary. Tune $\gamma$ and $C$ jointly by cross-validation.

stem: How is the best split of a node chosen in a classification tree?
correct: The split with the largest drop in impurity such as Gini or entropy.
The purest children on average.

distractors.text: By the split that puts the same number of observations in each child.
By the split on the feature with the largest mean.
By the split with the smallest training error across the whole tree.
distractors.misconception: describes a global search, not greedy splitting

distractors.text: By a random choice among the features.
distractors.misconception: describes extra randomisation, not the rule

distractors.text: By the split that maximises the number of leaves.

explanation: For class proportions $p_k$, Gini is $1-\sum p_k^2$ and entropy $-\sum p_k\log p_k$; both are zero at a pure node.

stem: How is a decision tree usually built?
correct: Greedily, one node at a time, with no global optimum guaranteed.
Top-down splits chosen locally.

distractors.text: By an exhaustive search that finds the globally optimal tree.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the global problem is intractable

distractors.text: Bottom-up, by merging leaves until one node remains.
By gradient descent on the tree's parameters.
By fitting a linear model in each node.
By sampling splits at random and keeping the best.

explanation: Finding the optimal tree is NP-hard, so CART uses greedy splitting and then prunes.

stem: Why are fully grown decision trees prone to overfitting, and what is the remedy?
correct: Tiny leaves fit noise (high variance); pruning or limiting depth helps.
Deep trees have high variance.

distractors.text: Deep trees have high bias, and the remedy is to grow them deeper.
Trees overfit because they ignore the training labels.
The remedy is to remove the validation set.
Trees never overfit, since splits are chosen on impurity.
The remedy is to standardise the features.

explanation: A tree with one observation per leaf has zero training error. Pruning picks the subtree with the best penalised or cross-validated error.

stem: What happens to a decision tree if a feature is replaced by a monotone transformation, such as its logarithm?
correct: Same splits and predictions, since only the ordering of values matters.
Trees are invariant to it.

distractors.text: The tree changes, since splits depend on the scale of the feature.
The tree gets deeper, since the transformed data are more spread out.
Only the root split changes.
distractors.misconception: gives a specific but false claim

distractors.text: The impurity becomes zero.
distractors.misconception: confuses the transformation with the labels

distractors.text: The tree can then no longer split on that feature.

explanation: Splits compare a value to a threshold, so any order-preserving transformation gives the same partitions. This is why trees need no feature scaling.

stem: What type of function does a regression tree produce?
correct: A piecewise constant function, so it cannot extrapolate a trend.
A step function with one value per leaf.

distractors.text: A piecewise linear function with continuous joints.
A smooth function with continuous derivatives.
A single global polynomial.
A function that increases with every feature.
A function that extrapolates the trend of the last leaf.

explanation: Each leaf predicts the mean of its training responses, so predictions beyond the data stay at the edge leaf's value.

stem: What is the main effect of bagging a high-variance learner?
correct: Averaging bootstrap models lowers variance, bias about the same.
It stabilises predictions.

distractors.text: It lowers bias but leaves variance unchanged.
It increases variance by adding randomness.
It always improves any learner, including linear regression.
distractors.misconception: forgets that stable learners gain little

distractors.text: It makes the model interpretable as a single tree.
It removes the need for a validation set.

explanation: Averaging $B$ identically distributed predictors with variance $\sigma^2$ and correlation $\rho$ has variance $\rho\sigma^2+(1-\rho)\sigma^2/B$.

stem: How does a random forest improve on bagged trees?
correct: Random feature subsets at each split decorrelate the trees.
Less correlation, so averaging helps more.

distractors.text: It lowers the bias of each tree by using all features at every split.
distractors.misconception: reverses what the feature subsets do

distractors.text: It grows trees sequentially, each correcting its predecessor.
It uses a single deep tree.
It increases the correlation between trees to share information.
It prunes each tree heavily.

explanation: With strongly predictive features, plain bagged trees all split on the same variable and stay correlated. Random subsets of size $m<p$ break this.

stem: How does boosting build its model?
correct: Weak learners are added in turn, each fitted to the current errors.
Mainly reduces bias.

distractors.text: It averages independent learners trained in parallel on bootstrap samples.
It fits one very deep tree and prunes it.
It reduces variance but never bias.
It cannot overfit, as every round improves the training fit.
It ignores the previous learners when fitting a new one.

explanation: Boosting fits the negative gradient of the loss; early stopping or shrinkage controls overfitting as rounds increase.

stem: What is the out-of-bag (OOB) error of a bagged ensemble?
correct: Each point is predicted only by trees that never saw it, then errors averaged.
A built-in test error estimate.

distractors.text: The error on observations that appear in every bootstrap sample.
distractors.misconception: reverses which points are out of the bag

distractors.text: The training error of the full ensemble.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the training error

distractors.text: The error on a held-out test set provided by the user.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a test set

distractors.text: The difference between the largest and smallest tree errors.
It is biased towards zero, since each point is used for training.
distractors.misconception: misses that OOB points were not used

explanation: About 37% of observations are left out of each bootstrap sample, so OOB predictions come from roughly a third of the trees.

stem: In gradient boosting, what is the role of the learning rate (shrinkage) $\nu$?
correct: It scales each tree's contribution; small $\nu$ needs more trees.
Small steps curb overfitting.

distractors.text: A large $\nu$ always generalises better, as it needs fewer trees.
It sets the depth of each tree.
It is the fraction of data used in each tree.
It must equal one for the boosting algorithm to converge.
It has no effect when early stopping is used.
distractors.misconception: ignores that it sets the pace of the path

explanation: Each round adds $\nu f_m(x)$. Lowering $\nu$ and increasing the number of rounds trades computation for accuracy.

stem: What does the naive Bayes classifier assume?
correct: Features are conditionally independent given the class.
The class-conditional density factorises.

distractors.text: Features are unconditionally independent of each other.
distractors.misconception: drops the conditioning on the class

distractors.text: Features are Gaussian with identical variance in each class.
distractors.misconception: describes a specific variant, not the assumption

distractors.text: The classes are equally likely a priori.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a uniform prior

distractors.text: The labels are independent of the features.
The features are all binary.
distractors.misconception: confuses the assumption with one variant

explanation: Under the assumption $p(x\mid y)=\prod_jp(x_j\mid y)$, estimation needs only one-dimensional densities. The class probabilities can still be well ranked even when the assumption is wrong.

stem: How do LDA and QDA differ?
correct: LDA shares one covariance (linear boundaries); QDA does not (quadratic).
Shared versus separate covariances.

distractors.text: LDA gives quadratic boundaries, and QDA linear ones.
Both assume diagonal covariances.
LDA does not assume normality, and QDA does.
QDA has fewer parameters than LDA.
LDA needs the classes to be equally likely.

explanation: QDA estimates a covariance matrix per class, so it has more variance and needs more data than LDA.

stem: How does a generative classifier compute the class probabilities $P(y\mid x)$?
correct: By Bayes' rule, density times prior.
$P(y=k\mid x)\propto p(x\mid y=k)\,\pi_k$, normalised over classes.

distractors.text: Directly from the likelihood $p(x\mid y)$ without a prior.
By fitting $P(y\mid x)$ with a parametric model, ignoring $p(x)$.
As the prior alone, since the features are noise.
By counting the neighbours of $x$ in each class.
By taking the class with the largest feature mean.

explanation: Generative models learn $p(x,y)$, so they can also be used to simulate data or to handle missing features.

stem: Which statement about the EM algorithm for a Gaussian mixture model is correct?
correct: It alternates soft assignments and updates, never lowering the likelihood.
May stop at a local maximum.

distractors.text: It converges to the global maximum from any start.
It assigns each point to exactly one component at each step.
The likelihood can decrease in some iterations.
It needs the true component labels.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the labels are latent

distractors.text: It fixes the covariances of all components to the identity.

explanation: $k$-means is the limiting case with equal spherical covariances and hard assignments.

stem: Why might a discriminative classifier such as logistic regression be preferred to a generative one?
correct: It models $P(y\mid x)$ directly, so it is more robust to wrong assumptions.
It needs no model for the distribution of the features.

distractors.text: It always has lower error than a generative model with any amount of data.
It can generate new feature vectors.
distractors.misconception: attributes a generative ability to it

distractors.text: It handles missing features naturally.
It needs fewer training points than naive Bayes.
It is unaffected by class imbalance.

explanation: Ng and Jordan: naive Bayes may reach its (higher) asymptotic error with fewer samples, while logistic regression has lower asymptotic error.

stem: What is the first principal component of a centred data matrix?
correct: The unit direction along which the projected data vary most.
The top eigenvector of the covariance.

distractors.text: The direction along which the data have minimum variance.
The direction most correlated with the label.
The feature with the largest mean.
The average of all the features.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a mean vector

distractors.text: The direction of the largest single entry.

explanation: PCA solves $\max_{\|v\|=1}v^\top Sv$; the maximum is the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ of $S$, with eigenvector $v_1$.

stem: How is the proportion of variance explained by the $j$th principal component computed?
correct: Its eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues.
$\lambda_j/\sum_k\lambda_k$ of the covariance matrix.

distractors.text: Its eigenvalue divided by the largest eigenvalue.
The square of its eigenvector divided by $p$.
The correlation of the component with the first one.
distractors.misconception: uses the correlation, which is zero

distractors.text: One divided by the number of components.
The sum of its loadings.

explanation: The sum of all eigenvalues is the total variance. The scree plot of $\lambda_j$ helps to choose the number of components.

stem: How are principal components related to the singular value decomposition $X=UDV^\top$ of a centred data matrix?
correct: Columns of $V$ are the principal directions, with variances $d_j^2/(n-1)$.
Scores are $UD$.

distractors.text: The columns of $U$ are the principal directions.
distractors.misconception: confuses the left and right singular vectors

distractors.text: The variances are the singular values $d_j$ themselves.
The decomposition is only available for square matrices.
The principal directions are the rows of $D$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the diagonal matrix with directions

distractors.text: PCA requires the data matrix to be uncentred.

explanation: $X^\top X=VD^2V^\top$, so the eigenvectors of the covariance are the columns of $V$.

stem: Why is the data centred (and often standardised) before PCA?
correct: Without centring the first component captures the mean; large units dominate.
PCA is driven by variances.

distractors.text: PCA requires every variable to have a normal distribution.
Centring makes the components correlated with each other.
Standardising is required for the SVD to exist.
Scaling has no effect on the components.
Centring makes the eigenvalues all equal.

explanation: Using the correlation matrix (standardised data) gives components that do not depend on the units. Covariance-based PCA is appropriate when variables share units.

stem: Which statement about t-SNE is correct?
correct: It keeps local neighbourhoods, but gaps and cluster sizes are unreliable.
Output depends on perplexity and seed.

distractors.text: It preserves global distances exactly.
It is a linear projection like PCA.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a linear method

distractors.text: It gives the same picture for every seed.
Cluster sizes in the plot reflect the sizes of the clusters in the data.
It can embed new data points without refitting.
distractors.misconception: overlooks the lack of an explicit mapping

explanation: t-SNE matches neighbour probabilities; global structure is distorted, so it is for exploration, not inference.

stem: What does the $k$-means algorithm do?
correct: It alternates assigning points to centroids and recomputing centroids.
Each step lowers the objective.

distractors.text: It finds the global minimum of the within-cluster sum of squares.
It chooses the number of clusters automatically.
It builds a tree of nested clusters.
It needs labelled data.
It maximises the distance between points in the same cluster.

explanation: Both steps cannot increase $\sum_i\|x_i-\mu_{c(i)}\|^2$; the algorithm terminates because the number of partitions is finite.

stem: Why can the within-cluster sum of squares not be used by itself to choose $k$?
correct: It always decreases as $k$ grows, reaching zero when every point is alone.
More clusters always fit better.

distractors.text: It increases with $k$, so the smallest $k$ is best.
It is independent of $k$.
It is only defined for $k=2$.
It is minimised at the true number of clusters.
distractors.misconception: confuses the objective with a model-selection criterion

distractors.text: It can only be computed on a test set.

explanation: The elbow, silhouette, gap statistic or a stability analysis helps to pick $k$. Domain knowledge matters too.

stem: How does the initialisation affect $k$-means?
correct: Different starts reach different local minima.
The result depends on the start, since the objective is non-convex.

distractors.text: The algorithm always reaches the same solution.
Initialisation affects only the speed, never the final clustering.
Starting with all centroids at the same point is best.
The objective is convex, so any start is fine.
Random starts are never useful.

explanation: $k$-means++ chooses seeds spread out with probability proportional to squared distance, giving an $O(\log k)$ approximation guarantee in expectation.

stem: What is a drawback of single linkage in hierarchical agglomerative clustering?
correct: Chaining: one close pair can merge two clusters into a straggly shape.
A bridge joins separate groups.

distractors.text: It always produces compact spherical clusters.
It needs the number of clusters in advance.
It is sensitive only to the farthest points.
It cannot produce a dendrogram.
It requires the data to be labelled.

explanation: Complete linkage uses the largest pairwise distance and tends to give compact clusters; average linkage is in between.

stem: When is spectral clustering preferable to $k$-means?
correct: When clusters are non-convex, since it uses a graph Laplacian eigenspace.
It separates concentric rings.

distractors.text: When the clusters are spherical and of equal size.
When the data have no similarity structure.
distractors.misconception: ignores that it needs a similarity graph

distractors.text: It is always faster than $k$-means.
It avoids the need to choose the number of clusters.
It uses only the Euclidean distance to centroids.

explanation: It builds a similarity graph, takes the first $k$ eigenvectors of the Laplacian, and runs $k$-means on those embedded points.

stem: What does the area under the ROC curve (AUC) measure?
correct: The chance a random positive is scored above a random negative.
Ranking quality over all thresholds.

distractors.text: The proportion of correct predictions at the 0.5 threshold.
The probability that the predicted probabilities are calibrated.
The precision of the classifier at the best threshold.
The expected profit of a trading rule.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with a financial metric

distractors.text: The proportion of positive labels in the data.

explanation: AUC is the Mann-Whitney statistic scaled to $[0,1]$. It is invariant to monotone transformations of the score, so it says nothing about calibration.

stem: What is calibration of a probabilistic classifier?
correct: Among cases given probability $p$, a fraction $p$ are positive.
Probabilities match frequencies.

distractors.text: The classifier has a high AUC.
The predicted probabilities sum to one for each class.
The classifier has equal error on both classes.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with balanced error rates

distractors.text: The training and test errors are equal.
Predicted probabilities are all close to 0 or 1.

explanation: A classifier can rank perfectly (AUC = 1) while its probabilities are far from the true frequencies. Platt scaling or isotonic regression recalibrates.

stem: Why can accuracy be misleading on a heavily imbalanced data set?
correct: Predicting the majority class gives high accuracy and finds no rare cases.
Rare-class recall matters more.

distractors.text: Accuracy is only defined for balanced data.
Accuracy always equals the AUC.
Imbalanced data make the precision undefined.
Accuracy overweights the minority class.
It is misleading only when there are more than two classes.

explanation: With 1% positives, "never predict positive" scores 99% accuracy. Use the precision-recall curve or cost-weighted metrics.

stem: Why is purged cross-validation used for financial labels built from overlapping future windows?
correct: Training samples whose label windows overlap the test period leak.
Overlap makes neighbours dependent.

distractors.text: Purging increases the amount of training data.
Overlapping labels make ordinary $k$-fold cross-validation too pessimistic.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the bias

distractors.text: It is needed only when the sample is small.
It shuffles observations so that the folds are i.i.d.
distractors.misconception: does the opposite of what is needed

distractors.text: It removes the need for a separate test set.

explanation: With a 5-day forward return label, a training point near the test boundary shares days with test labels. Purging and an embargo prevent that leakage.

stem: Which practice is appropriate for validating a model on financial time series?
correct: Use time-ordered splits like walk-forward, training before evaluation.
Test only on later data.

distractors.text: Use random shuffled $k$-fold splits to make the folds identically distributed.
Select the model with the best in-sample Sharpe ratio.
Tune on the test period and report the best result.
Always train on the most recent data only.
distractors.misconception: gives a fixed rule that is not generally valid

distractors.text: Use the future to standardise the features.

explanation: Returns have a very low signal-to-noise ratio and non-stationary structure, so random splits that mix past and future flatter any model.
